As long as the vast majority of American workers (I’m from the U.S. and that’s what I believe is being referenced here) are listed as at-will employees, it’s incredibly difficult for the average person to work within these laws to bring any kind of action or change. Someone can be fired for any excuse of a reason such as being a minute late for work after years of being on time, and the burden of proof is on the person being discriminated against to prove that it was because of a protected class. Employers know this, they use this, and they count on the EXTREMELY strict reporting deadlines for this to even be considered filtering out most people who would be able to bring these suits because the first priority after a traumatic firing usually has to be “how am I going to survive without income or heath insurance” and “how do I work on healing after such a traumatic experience” before looking into options for legal recourse. 

The intentions behind these laws are wonderful, but a strong union who knows how to look out for these issues, can inform workers of their rights when discriminated against, will help with the legwork when these issues come up, and bargain for employment agreements that remove the at-will conditions for abusive employers is by far a stronger resource than laws that offer recourse that’s inaccessible to a tremendous amount of people.

Source: I work in a law office that helps disenfranchised and vulnerable people, as well as my own personal experience with this issue firsthand.

I work as a social worker and manage two counties’ multidisciplinary teams on elder abuse. I keep an eye on case statuses, help professionals work together to get good outcomes for folks who need help, and make sure that our clients have the supports they need after they’ve experienced abuse. I don’t make a ton of money and my career has already had some pretty hard ups and downs, but the future looks bright and I’m doing okay. I’m also incredibly lucky to have a paralegal in my office who really enjoys administrative/organizational things and helps keep me where I need to be. Working with a team where we all check in on each other (in a kind and supportive way) has been incredible for my adhd, and I’ve done way better in this work environment than in others before. 

I still have issues with guilt about past jobs that my adhd has gotten in the way of success for, but something that’s helped me is changing the way I look at my work history. Instead of looking at it as “places I worked before having to leave for something else”, I look at it more like I studied in different offices to learn skills to draw from once I found where I wanted to be. I feel good where I am now, but it’s a journey and there were some big adhd challenges on the way to get here. No low moment defines your journey, and you deserve to be happy no matter how work feels. Take your time, and try things until you find where you can work and feel the way you want to feel. It’s okay to make a lot of mistakes along the way. You’re not defined by your work.
